newsitem.title: POLAND: President signs bill to vet Polish officials' past.
newsitem.headline: President signs bill to vet Polish officials' past.

text.p: Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said on Wednesday he had signed, despite misgivings, a bill requiring top public officials to be screened for past ties with communist-era police.

His decision, defying the wishes of his close political allies, the ex-communists, opened the way to inquiries into the past of candidates in parliamentary elections which Kwasniewski set for September 21.

"I signed today the law on revealing work or service in the state security organs, or cooperation with them in the years 1944-90, by people filling public functions," Kwasniewski said in a televised address.

Under the new law, those seeking elected posts and senior positions in the government, judiciary or public media would have to declare whether they had been workers or informants for the security police under communist rule, which was toppled in 1989.
Unlike some ex-Soviet bloc countries, Poland has not yet formally opened up communist security police files.

Kwasniewski said he had reservations about the final version of the law, which he initiated but was considerably altered by parliament. He said the law now had shortcomings that Poles could come to regret.

"Above all, it lacks an unambiguous definition of the concept of secret collaboration with the special services, which could bring a situation that wrongs people subjected to vetting," Kwasniewski said.

He also criticised the fact that citizens would not have clear legally defined access to their files, and that these would not be separated from interior ministry archives. Kwasniewski said that might allow abuse of records arising from political disputes.
He said he would ask parliament to amend the law on these matters.
The president said, however, that it was necessary to reveal the truth about the past and help those who were accused of security police collaboration but were innocent to clear their names.

Supporters of the bill say former security service agents have taken key state jobs, leaving them open to blackmail. Opponents, mainly ex-communists, argue it is too late to start opening files that are also unreliable.
They also say the bill may harm Poland's intelligence and counter-intelligence services by exposing its agents.
Kwasniewski called for people who had worked for these services, in the belief that they were serving Poland, to be treated differently from those linked with the security police.
"They cannot be assessed in the same way," he said.
The law sets up a special court to probe whether candidates for senior public posts collaborated with the communist police. Current incumbents are also expected to come clean.
Candidates will face up to five years in prison, stiff fines and a ban from selected posts if the court finds they had lied to obtained their posts.
But a declaration that they had collaborated would not automatically block their way to such posts.
The vetting bill was approved in parliament earlier this year when the Peasant Party in the ruling coalition joined with the opposition to out-vote its ex-communist partners.

The coming elections will pit the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), the largest party in the coalition government, against groups rooted in the Solidarity movement that toppled the old regime but lost power four years later.
